cues.text: A Young Priest in Madrid
Josemaría Escrivá , born in Barbastro, Spain, in 1902, was ordained a priest in 1925 and moved to Madrid to pursue a doctorate in civil law.
All the while, he sensed, as he later described it, an unclear but persistent call from God to some particular mission he could not yet identify.
In Madrid he ministered among the poor and sick in the city's poorest neighborhoods while continuing his studies.
The Foundational Vision
On October 2, 1928 , while making a retreat at a house of the Vincentian Fathers on Madrid’s outskirts, Escrivá experienced what he described as a divine illumination.
In it, he 'saw' Opus Dei — a new path within the Church calling ordinary lay Christians in every walk of life and profession.
It called them to seek holiness through everyday work and family responsibilities, rather than leaving secular life for the cloister.
Founding Members and Early Growth
Escrivá began sharing this vision through spiritual direction with small groups of students and young professionals in Madrid, among them the railway engineer Isidoro Zorzano.

In 1930, he understood that the message was intended for women as well, and by 1933 the first center, the DYA Academy offering law and architecture classes, opened in Madrid, blending professional formation with the spiritual message of Opus Dei.
Surviving the Spanish Civil War

The Spanish Civil War beginning in 1936 brought severe anti-Catholic persecution, forcing Escrivá and members of Opus Dei in Republican-controlled areas into hiding or exile for their safety; the founder eventually crossed the Pyrenees via Andorra to reach Nationalist-held territory.
After the war, he returned to Madrid in 1939 and Opus Dei's work resumed and expanded to other Spanish cities.
Official Recognition
The Bishop of Madrid granted Opus Dei its first diocesan approval in 1941, and the Holy See granted definitive pontifical approval in 1950 under Pope Pius XII.

Decades later, in 1982, Pope John Paul II established Opus Dei as the Catholic Church's first personal prelature — a structure allowing it to operate across diocesan boundaries worldwide under its own prelate.
Legacy
Escrivá died in Rome in 1975 and was canonized by Pope John Paul II in 2002.
Opus Dei's core teaching — that ordinary work, faithfully and lovingly performed, can itself become a path to sanctity — has become one of the most influential expressions of lay spirituality.
The Second Vatican Council later emphasized this spirituality through its universal call to holiness, and the prelature today counts tens of thousands of members across the world.
